about.title: Alhambra Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Alhambra's shopping and dining blocks along Main Street, Valley Boulevard and Mission Road keep sidewalks, storefronts and parking structures busy well into the evening. Most visits end without incident. When one doesn't, whether it's a wet floor near a market entrance, a broken step at an apartment complex or a dim stairwell in a garage, California premises liability law asks whether the property owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and failed to fix it or warn you. That element, called notice, is where many claims are won or lost. Proof fades quickly: spills get mopped, businesses overwrite camera footage within days, and witnesses move on. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect people injured in Alhambra with an independent attorney who handles premises cases in Los Angeles County. The connection costs nothing, and the attorney works on contingency, so there is no fee unless your claim results in a recovery. You generally have two years to file, and less when a public entity owns the property.

items.title: Notice Is the Heart of the Case
items.desc: California does not hold owners liable simply because someone fell. The attorney you're connected with will focus on showing the owner knew or should have known about the hazard and left it unaddressed.

items.title: Evidence Disappears Fast
items.desc: Surveillance systems at Alhambra stores and garages often overwrite footage in a matter of days. An early preservation request, along with photos of the hazard and your shoes, can keep that evidence from vanishing.

items.title: Deadlines and Shared Fault Matter
items.desc: Most claims must be filed within two years, and the window is much shorter if a city or other public entity owns the property. Under California's pure comparative fault rule, being partly responsible reduces a recovery but does not erase it.

items.question: I slipped inside a grocery store on Valley Boulevard and the manager wrote up a report. Is that enough?
items.answer: A store incident report is a start, but it's written from the business's point of view and you may never see it. Take your own photos of the floor, any signage, and your footwear, and get names of anyone who saw you fall. Then ask, in writing, that the store preserve its camera footage from that day, because many systems erase it within a week or two.

items.question: The property owner says the hazard was obvious and I should have seen it. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: Not in California. The state uses pure comparative fault, which means a jury or adjuster can assign you a share of responsibility and reduce your compensation by that percentage. Even if you're found partly at fault, you can still recover the remaining portion.

items.question: What if I fell on a cracked sidewalk or in a public building in Alhambra?
items.answer: When a public entity owns or controls the property, the rules change. You typically have to submit a formal claim to the entity first, and the deadline to do so is considerably shorter than the two years that apply to private owners. Because of that, it's wise to talk with an attorney soon after the fall rather than waiting to see how your injuries develop.
